catalog_quote: Both Wapishana and Mawayana have intensity stress, placed on the penultimate mora of a phonological word (i.e., if the final syllable is CV, then the penultimate syllable is stressed; if the final syllable is CVC or CVV, the final syllable is stressed; cf. Wapishana /pɨtɨkapa/ ‘look!’ [ˌpɨtɨˈkapa] and /pɨtɨkapan/ ‘you see, you look’ [pɨˌtɨkaˈpan]). [...] In Mawayana, in contrast, secondary stress falls on even-numbered CV syllables from the beginning to the end of the word (/wa-katuku-sɨ/ [wa.ˌkaː.tu.ˈkuː.sɨ] ‘our club, stick’); non-CV syllables are always stressed (/awjaɗa/ [ˈaw.ja.ɗa] ‘toucan sp.’). Unlike Wapishana, Mawayana stress is thus sensitive to prefixes, not suffixes (e.g., /kanawa/ [ka.ˈnaː.wa] ‘canoe’, /wa-kanawa/ [wa.ˈkaː.na.wa] ‘our canoe’). Stressed vowels are usually lengthened; unstressed vowels, though unlengthened, do not reduce or disappear, unlike Wapishana unstressed vowels. The same pattern is attested in Cariban languages, including neighboring Waiwai. As the previous paragraph has already shown, the attested syllable types in both languages are CV, CVV (VV being either a long vowel or two different vowels, always stressed on the first vowel: /ai/ = [ˈai] = [aj], not [aˈi]) or CVN, where N is a nasal coda consonant. [p. 80:] the Wapishana and the Mawayana systems differ in directionality: the former counts syllables from the end of the word, while the latter counts syllables from the beginning of the word.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Cariban-type rhythmic (iambic) stress computed left-to-right over the phonological word, prefixes included: every even-numbered light (CV) syllable from the left is stressed and its vowel lengthened; heavy syllables (CVV, CVN) are always stressed; unstressed vowels are not reduced. The rightmost rhythmic beat is transcribed as primary ([wa.ˌkaː.tu.ˈkuː.sɨ]); a word-final light syllable is not stressed in the examples. Meira's blanket statement that primary stress is on the 'penultimate mora' in both languages fits [ji.ˈmaː.ɗa], [ka.ˈnaː.wa], [wa.ˌkaː.tu.ˈkuː.sɨ] but not his own [wa.ˈkaː.na.wa] (antepenult), so the operative Mawayana rule is the left-to-right count plus weight; on p. 80 he says Mawayana 'counts syllables from the beginning of the word', 'corresponds exactly to the rhythmic stress system found in Cariban languages' (Waiwai, Tiriyó) and was probably borrowed from Cariban.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Explicitly described: secondary stress on even-numbered CV syllables counted from the word beginning; non-CV syllables always stressed (e.g. [wa.ˌkaː.tu.ˈkuː.sɨ]).
new_statements.exceptions: Heavy (non-CV: CVV, CVN) syllables are always stressed regardless of count ([ˈaw.ja.ɗa]); VV sequences stressed on the first vowel ([ˈai], not [aˈi]); some phonetic long vowels may be underlying rather than stress-induced ('Mawayana appears to have some [long vowels] as well, but most cases of phonetic long vowels are the result of stress'). Internal tension between the 'penultimate mora' generalization and the example [wa.ˈkaː.na.wa].
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word including person prefixes (wa- 'our' shifts the count: [ka.ˈnaː.wa] vs [wa.ˈkaː.na.wa]); examples are citation forms from the author's 1997 field data (speaker Tenetene, Waiwai village of Mapuera, Pará, Brazil).
new_statements.identity_note: Meira 2019 describes Mawayana proper (Glottolog mapi1252 'Mapidian-Mawayana', ISO mpw; SAPhon and older ISO usage code it mzx). His primary data come from one elderly speaker (Tenetene) in the Waiwai village of Mapuera, Pará, Brazil (1997), supplemented by Howard's 1985-86 Kaxmi (Roraima) questionnaire and Carlin's Suriname (Kwamalasamutu, Trio village) materials; Coretta 2013 and Michels 2014 are based solely on Carlin's Suriname recordings. All are treated as one language; Meira notes the last speakers live among Waiwai and Tiriyó and attributes the left-to-right rhythmic stress to Cariban contact.
